title: Manage AI Vulnerabilities and Asset Posture
intro: Managing AI weaknesses before attackers find them: keeping model vulnerability and exposure registers; prioritising findings by context and consequence rather than base score alone; patching AI pipelines, frameworks, open-source components and models safely; protecting legacy models that can’t be fixed with compensating controls and strict usage restrictions; and running continuous security reviews with posture metrics that show real progress.
objectives: Maintain vulnerability and exposure registers for AI models and components, from discovery through verified closure
Prioritise AI vulnerabilities using exposure, exploitation, data sensitivity, privileges, existing controls and consequence
Run inventory-driven patch management for AI pipelines, dependencies, open-source components and models
Apply compensating controls, usage restrictions and time-limited exceptions to legacy models
Run continuous AI security reviews and report meaningful posture assurance metrics to governance

scenes.title: Knowing your weak spots
scenes.say: You can’t manage weaknesses you haven’t written down. AI systems add new kinds of weakness to the usual software flaws, and they change quickly. | This video covers model vulnerability and exposure registers: what goes in them, where the findings come from, and how entries move from discovery to closure.

scenes.title: What belongs in an AI vulnerability register

items.d: Sensitive data reachable via the model

scenes.say: An AI vulnerability register covers six kinds of weakness. | Model weaknesses, such as susceptibility to jailbreaks or prompt injection found in testing. | Flaws in components: published vulnerabilities in serving frameworks, orchestration tools and libraries. | Misconfigurations, such as model endpoints open to the internet or protected by weak authentication. | Data exposures, where sensitive data can be reached through the model or its retrieval system. | Supply chain issues, such as unsigned models or files in formats that can run code when loaded. | And agent permission risks, where agents hold more tools or scopes than they need.

scenes.title: Vulnerability and exposure registers
rows: Where assets can be reached, and by whom
scenes.say: Two related records work together. | A vulnerability register records weaknesses in models and components. An exposure register records where AI assets can be reached, and by whom. | For example, a vulnerability might be that a model follows role-play jailbreaks. An exposure might be that its endpoint can be reached from the internet without authentication. | The first answers: what is wrong? The second answers: who could exploit it? Put them together, and you know how urgent each weakness really is.

scenes.title: The life of a register entry
scenes.say: Every register entry follows the same life cycle. It is discovered: by scanning, red teaming, a bug bounty report, monitoring or a published advisory. | It is recorded with the affected asset and exact version, a description and the evidence needed to reproduce it. | It is assessed for severity in context, which the next video covers. | It is assigned an owner and a due date that matches its priority. | It is treated: fixed, mitigated with compensating controls, or formally accepted by the risk owner. | And it is verified by retesting before it is closed, so nobody closes an entry just because a ticket was marked done.

scenes.title: Where findings come from

items.d: Adversarial testing of models and agents

scenes.say: Findings come from six main sources. | Public advisories, such as CVE records, the open source vulnerability database and vendor security bulletins. | Scanning of dependencies, container images and model files. | Red teaming: adversarial testing of models, retrieval systems and agents. | Bug bounty programmes and coordinated disclosure from external researchers. | Monitoring and incidents, which reveal weaknesses in production. | And AI threat knowledge bases, such as MITRE ATLAS, the AI Vulnerability Database and OWASP’s AI projects.

items: Register model, component, configuration, data, supply chain and agent weaknesses
Pair vulnerabilities with exposures to judge urgency
Discover, record, assess, assign, treat, verify
Feed the register from advisories, scans, red teams and incidents
scenes.say: To recap. | Register weaknesses in models, components, configurations, data, the supply chain and agent permissions. | Pair each vulnerability with its exposure, to judge how urgent it really is. | Move every entry through discovery, recording, assessment, assignment, treatment and verification. | And feed the register from advisories, scanning, red teams, researchers and incidents.

blocks.md:
### Register fields
| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **ID and title** | Unique reference, linked to tickets and the risk register |
| **Affected assets and versions** | Model name and version (or hash), application, component and version, environment; taken from the AI inventory and AIBOM (Module 6.3) |
| **Category** | Mapping to OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, MITRE ATLAS technique, or CWE for software flaws |
| **Description and evidence** | What the weakness is and how to reproduce it, stored securely, because evidence may itself be sensitive (Module 6.5) |
| **Source and date** | Scan, red team, bug bounty, advisory, incident; when it was found |
| **Exposure** | Who can reach the asset: internet, authenticated users, internal only; agent privileges and data reachable |
| **Severity** | Base score plus contextual priority (Section 2) |
| **Owner and due date** | Accountable owner and target date set by priority |
| **Treatment and status** | Fix, mitigate, accept (with approver and expiry) or transfer; open, in progress, verified, closed |
| **Residual risk** | What remains after treatment, reflected in the risk register |

### Vulnerabilities versus model limitations
Not every model behaviour is a security vulnerability. Hallucinations, limited accuracy or occasional bias are **limitations** that belong in quality and risk management, unless an attacker can **reliably trigger** them to cause harm, or they bypass a security control (Module 6.5 covers this distinction). Record both, but route them to the right owners.

### Sources of AI vulnerability information
- **CVE** and the **NVD**, **OSV** (open source vulnerability data, including Python packages) and GitHub security advisories, which increasingly cover AI frameworks, serving platforms and agent tools.
- **Vendor bulletins** from model providers, GPU vendors and platform providers.
- **Model hub scanning:** hubs scan uploaded files for malicious code and unsafe serialisation formats (Module 3.7).
- **AI-specific knowledge bases:** MITRE ATLAS (techniques and case studies), the AI Vulnerability Database (AVID) and OWASP’s generative AI security projects.
- **Internal sources:** red teaming (Module 6.4), bug bounties that include AI systems, security reviews, monitoring and incidents.

Keep the register **connected**: AI inventory and AIBOM entries let you match a new advisory to every affected deployment in minutes, rather than asking teams by email.

blocks.title: Vulnerability or exposure?
pairs: The model reveals its system prompt when asked in another language
Vulnerability
The inference endpoint accepts requests from any internet address
Exposure
The serving framework version has a published remote code execution flaw
Vulnerability
An agent with refund rights is available to anonymous website visitors
Exposure
The model file uses a format that can execute code when loaded
Vulnerability (supply chain)

blocks.title: Register questions
blocks.md: A good register records **exact assets and versions**, **evidence**, **exposure**, **owner and due date**, and requires **verification before closure**. It is fed by many sources and linked to the **inventory and AIBOM**, so new advisories can be matched quickly. Spreadsheets nobody owns, or entries closed without retesting, are common wrong answers.

q.q: A critical advisory is published for an open-source LLM serving framework. The security team has to email every development team to ask whether they use it, and answers take two weeks. What would MOST improve this?
o: A policy banning open-source serving frameworks across the organisation
An AI inventory and AIBOM linked to the register, so advisories match assets
A weekly meeting where development teams list the frameworks they are using
A subscription to more vulnerability advisory feeds for the security team
q.why: Linking the register to an accurate inventory and AIBOM lets the team match a new advisory to every affected deployment immediately. Bans, meetings and more feeds don’t tell you where the component is running.

scenes.title: Fix what matters first
scenes.sub: Prioritising AI vulnerabilities by context and consequence
scenes.say: Most organisations have far more vulnerabilities than time to fix them. A severity score on its own can’t tell you which ones matter most in your environment. | This video covers prioritising AI vulnerabilities by context and consequence.

scenes.title: Same flaw, different priority
scenes.say: Here is the same vulnerability, in the same serving framework, in two places. | One deployment is an internal batch model reachable only from the internal network. The other is a public agent that anyone on the internet can talk to. | The batch model processes synthetic test data. The agent handles customer records. | The batch model is read-only, with no tools. The agent can send email and issue refunds. | So the batch model can wait for the next patch window, while the public agent needs an emergency fix within days. Same score, very different consequence.

scenes.title: Context factors

items.d: Who can reach it, and how easily
What already blocks or detects it

scenes.say: Six context factors turn a generic score into a real priority. | Exposure: who can reach the system, and how easily. | Exploitation: is the vulnerability known to be exploited in the wild, or likely to be soon? | Data sensitivity: what the system can see, including what its retrieval and tools can reach. | Privileges and agency: what the system can do, especially agents that act in other systems. | Existing controls: guardrails, isolation or monitoring that already block or detect exploitation. | And business consequence: harm to people’s safety, money, legal obligations and reputation.

scenes.title: Exploitability and consequence
scenes.say: A simple way to combine the factors is to place each finding on two axes: how easy it is to exploit in your context, and how severe the consequence would be. | Easy to exploit with severe consequences: act now, and fix within days, using compensating controls in the meantime. | Hard to exploit but with severe consequences: fix soon, and add controls that make exploitation even harder. | Easy to exploit but with limited consequences: fix soon, and monitor for attempts. | And hard to exploit with limited consequences: handle in the routine patch cycle.

scenes.title: Scoring tools to know

items.d: Emerging scoring for agentic AI risks

scenes.say: Several scoring tools help. | CVSS version four separates base severity from threat and environmental metrics, so you can adjust for your context. | The exploit prediction scoring system estimates how likely a vulnerability is to be exploited soon. | CISA’s known exploited vulnerabilities catalogue lists flaws attackers are already using. | Stakeholder-specific vulnerability categorisation uses a decision tree that ends in track, attend or act. | OWASP’s AI vulnerability scoring system is an emerging approach for agentic AI risks. | And your own business impact analysis tells you the consequence of each system failing.

items: A base score is a starting point, not a priority
Weigh exposure, exploitation, data, privileges, controls and consequence
Known exploited and agentic, internet-facing systems go first
Use CVSS, EPSS, KEV and SSVC together
scenes.say: To recap. | A base severity score is a starting point, not a priority. | Weigh exposure, exploitation, data sensitivity, privileges, existing controls and business consequence. | Vulnerabilities known to be exploited, in internet-facing systems with agency or sensitive data, go to the front of the queue. | And use CVSS, EPSS, the known exploited catalogue and decision frameworks such as SSVC together.

blocks.md:
### Why context matters for AI
AI systems concentrate risk: a single model endpoint may reach large volumes of sensitive data through retrieval, and agents can act in many systems. The same flaw can be trivial in an isolated batch model and critical in an internet-facing agent with tools. Prioritise by **exploitability in context** and **consequence**, not by base score alone.

### Context factors in practice
| Factor | Questions to ask |
|---|---|
| **Exposure** | Internet-facing or internal? Authenticated? Who are the users? Can external content reach the model (retrieval, email, web)? |
| **Exploitation** | Listed in CISA KEV? High EPSS? Public exploit code? Seen in threat intelligence? |
| **Data sensitivity** | Personal, health, financial or confidential data in prompts, retrieval, memory or training data? |
| **Privileges and agency** | Tools, scopes and downstream systems; can it act without approval? Blast radius if hijacked? |
| **Existing controls** | Isolation, guardrails, output validation, rate limits, monitoring, human review |
| **Consequence** | Safety, financial loss, regulatory breach, reputation, number of people affected; criticality from the business impact analysis |

### Scoring frameworks
- **CVSS v4.0** (FIRST, 2023): Base metrics describe the flaw; **Threat** metrics (exploit maturity) and **Environmental** metrics (your security requirements and mitigations) adjust it. Supplemental metrics add context such as automatability.
- **EPSS** (FIRST): a daily estimate of the probability that a CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days.
- **CISA KEV:** a catalogue of vulnerabilities known to be exploited. In 2025 it included an unauthenticated code execution flaw in Langflow, a popular low-code tool for building AI agents (CVE-2025-3248).
- **SSVC** (CERT/CC and CISA): a decision tree using exploitation status, exposure, automatability and impact, leading to *Track*, *Track**, *Attend* or *Act*.
- **OWASP AIVSS:** an emerging AI vulnerability scoring system, focused first on agentic AI risks such as model manipulation, data poisoning and agent misalignment, with AI-specific metrics alongside CVSS-style base and environmental factors.

### Turning priority into deadlines
Set remediation targets by priority, not just severity: for example, known exploited and internet-facing within days; high priority within two to four weeks; others in the routine cycle. When a deadline can’t be met, apply **compensating controls** (Section 4) and record a time-limited exception approved by the risk owner.

blocks.title: Two findings, one engineer
blocks.md: A team has one engineer available this week. Finding A: a "critical" (CVSS 9.8) flaw in a document conversion library used only by an internal, offline batch job that processes public reports. Finding B: a "high" (CVSS 7.5) flaw in the serving framework behind the company’s customer-facing support agent, which has refund tools. Finding B is listed in CISA’s KEV catalogue.

q.q: Which finding should the engineer address FIRST, and why?
o: Finding A, because its CVSS base score is higher than Finding B’s score
Finding B, because it is known to be exploited and sits on an exposed agent with tools
Finding A, because libraries are easier to patch than serving frameworks
Neither, until the security team has assessed every other open finding first
q.why: Known exploitation, internet exposure and agency with financial tools make Finding B far more urgent in context. Base score alone, ease of patching or waiting for a full review are poor ways to prioritise.

blocks.title: Prioritisation questions
blocks.md: When a question compares vulnerabilities, look beyond the **base score** to **exploitation status** (KEV, EPSS), **exposure**, **data and privileges** and **business consequence**. Internet-facing agents with tools and sensitive data, plus known exploitation, almost always come first.

q.q: Which combination of factors should raise an AI vulnerability’s priority the MOST?
o: A high base score in a model used only in an isolated research lab
Known exploitation, internet exposure and an agent able to act in other systems
A medium base score in a model whose vendor has announced a patch for next year
A low base score, but a large number of affected internal test environments
q.why: Known exploitation plus exposure plus agency means the flaw is likely to be used and would cause real harm. The other combinations lack either likelihood or consequence.

sections.title: Patch management for AI pipelines and dependencies

scenes.title: Keeping the AI stack patched
scenes.sub: Patch management for pipelines, dependencies and open-source components
scenes.say: AI systems are built from a deep stack of fast-moving, often open-source components. Many have had serious vulnerabilities, and attackers have exploited some of them quickly. | This video covers patch management for AI pipelines, dependencies and open-source components.

scenes.title: The AI patch surface
scenes.say: The AI patch surface has six layers. | Hardware, drivers and operating systems, including GPU drivers and CUDA libraries. | Containers and images, with their base images and system packages. | Frameworks and serving: training libraries and inference servers. | Libraries and agent tooling: orchestration frameworks, connectors and MCP servers. | Models themselves: provider versions, fine-tunes and open-weight models, which receive updates too. | And pipelines: the CI actions, runners and build tools that produce everything else.

scenes.title: AI components under attack
scenes.say: Recent history shows why this matters. | In 2024, researchers reported attackers exploiting exposed Ray clusters, a popular framework for distributed AI workloads, in a campaign called ShadowRay. | Also in 2024, a path traversal flaw in Ollama, a tool for running models locally, could lead to remote code execution. | In 2025, PyTorch fixed a flaw that let malicious model files run code even when loaded with its safer loading option. | Langflow, a low-code tool for building AI agents, had an unauthenticated code execution flaw that CISA added to its known exploited catalogue. | And researchers showed a chain of flaws in NVIDIA’s Triton Inference Server that could let a remote, unauthenticated attacker take over the server.

scenes.title: A patch process for AI
scenes.say: A patch process for AI has six steps. It starts with an inventory: software and AI bills of materials, showing every component and version in every deployment. | Advisories are monitored and matched automatically to the inventory. | Each match is prioritised by context and consequence. | Patches are tested: functional tests for software, plus model evaluations, because a framework update can change model behaviour. | Rollout is staged: a canary first, then wider, with health and safety metrics watched. | And the result is verified and recorded, with the previous version kept ready for rollback.

scenes.title: Patching software and updating models
rows: Code; behaviour should stay the same
scenes.say: Patching software and updating models are different. | A software patch changes code, and behaviour should stay the same. A model update changes weights, and behaviour will change. | Software patches need functional and security tests. Model updates need quality, safety and fairness evaluations. | The main risk of a software patch is a breaking change. The main risk of a model update is a regression in safety or accuracy. | And rollback means reinstalling the previous package version, or redeploying the previous signed model version.

items: Patch every layer: drivers, images, frameworks, tooling, models, pipelines
Match advisories to an SBOM and AIBOM automatically
Test software functionally and models with evaluations
Stage rollouts; keep rollback ready; use virtual patches meanwhile
scenes.say: To recap. | Patch every layer of the AI stack: drivers, images, frameworks, agent tooling, models and pipelines. | Match advisories automatically against software and AI bills of materials. | Test software functionally, and test model behaviour with evaluations. | And stage rollouts with rollback ready, using virtual patches such as gateway rules while a fix is prepared.

blocks.md:
### Know what you run
- **SBOM and AIBOM:** generate bills of materials for every build, including Python packages, system libraries, containers, models and datasets. CycloneDX (including its machine learning BOM) and SPDX 3.0 (with AI and dataset profiles) support AI components (Module 6.3).
- **Pin and verify:** pin versions and hashes for packages, base images, models and CI actions, so you know exactly what changed when you patch (Module 3.7).
- **Use controlled sources:** internal package mirrors and model registries let you block known-bad versions centrally.

### Recent examples
| Component | Issue | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Ray** (distributed AI computing) | CVE-2023-48022: unauthenticated job submission. The vendor disputed it, saying Ray should only run in trusted networks, but exposed clusters were exploited in the "ShadowRay" campaign reported in 2024 | Exposure turns a design assumption into a vulnerability |
| **Ollama** (local model runner) | CVE-2024-37032 ("Probllama"): path traversal leading to code execution, fixed in 2024 | Popular tools spread fast and get exposed accidentally |
| **PyTorch** | CVE-2025-32434: code execution through malicious model files even with `weights_only=True`, fixed in version 2.6.0 | Loading untrusted models is risky; prefer safetensors and keep frameworks patched |
| **Langflow** (agent builder) | CVE-2025-3248: unauthenticated code execution, fixed in 1.3.0 and added to CISA KEV in May 2025 | Agent-building tools are internet-facing targets |
| **NVIDIA Triton Inference Server** | CVE-2025-23319 and related flaws in the Python backend, chainable to remote takeover by an unauthenticated attacker; fixed in release 25.07 | Inference servers hold models and data worth stealing |

### Patching well
- **Prioritise by context** (Section 2) and set target timescales by priority.
- **Test both behaviour and function:** framework, driver or tokenizer updates can subtly change model outputs, so run evaluation suites, including safety regression tests, before rollout (Module 5.6).
- **Stage rollouts:** canary or shadow deployments, with automatic rollback on error, latency or safety metric breaches (Module 6.2).
- **Rebuild, don’t patch in place:** rebuild containers from patched base images through the pipeline, so production matches what was tested.
- **Hosted models:** track provider deprecation schedules and security notices, pin versions, and test replacements before forced migrations.
- **Virtual patching:** when a fix isn’t possible yet, block the vulnerable path at the gateway or network, restrict exposure and increase monitoring (Section 4).
- **Emergency path:** for known exploited, internet-facing flaws, use the emergency change process (Module 5.1), with review afterwards.

blocks.title: Patch management terms
cards: SBOM
Software bill of materials: a machine-readable list of the components and versions in a build.
AIBOM
AI bill of materials: an SBOM extended to models, datasets and AI-specific dependencies.
Virtual patch
A control that blocks exploitation of a flaw, such as a gateway rule, while the real fix is prepared.
Safety regression test
An evaluation run before release to confirm an update hasn’t weakened safety behaviour.
safetensors
A model file format that stores weights without executable code, unlike Python pickle-based formats.

blocks.title: Patch questions
blocks.md: Look for **inventory-driven** patching (SBOM and AIBOM), **context-based prioritisation**, **testing that includes model evaluations**, **staged rollout with rollback** and **virtual patching** when a fix must wait. Patching production directly without testing, or waiting for the next quarterly cycle for a known exploited flaw, are wrong answers.

q.q: A security patch for the inference framework behind a customer chatbot is released. Which rollout approach is BEST?
o: Apply it directly to all production servers at once, to close the flaw as fast as possible
Test functionally and with model evaluations, then canary it with rollback ready
Wait for the next quarterly maintenance window, to reduce the number of changes
Ask the vendor to apply the patch on the organisation’s behalf when it has capacity
q.why: Testing both function and model behaviour, then rolling out gradually with rollback ready, closes the flaw quickly without risking a broken or less safe chatbot. Direct production changes skip testing, quarterly waits leave it exposed, and handing it to the vendor gives up control.

sections.title: Compensating controls and restrictions for legacy models

scenes.title: When you can’t fix it
scenes.sub: Compensating controls and usage restrictions for legacy models
scenes.say: Some AI systems can’t simply be patched or replaced. The model is out of support, retraining would take months, or a regulator validated this exact version. | This video covers compensating controls and strict usage restrictions for legacy models.

scenes.title: Why legacy models stay in service
scenes.say: Legacy models stay in service for six common reasons. | The vendor has ended support, so no more fixes are coming. | Replacement is expensive, because the model needs retraining or the platform needs rebuilding. | A regulator validated this exact version, and re-approval takes time and money. | The original training data has been lost or can no longer legally be used. | The model is embedded in devices or third-party integrations. | And critical business processes depend on it, so switching it off isn’t an option yet.

scenes.title: Compensating controls around a legacy model

layers.label: Isolation
layers.sub: Separate network segment, no internet, no new integrations

layers.label: Restricted access
layers.sub: Named users, strong authentication, no anonymous use

layers.label: Modern guardrails in front
layers.sub: Input filtering, output validation at a gateway

layers.label: Heightened monitoring
layers.sub: Tighter thresholds, full logging, rate limits

layers.label: Human review
layers.sub: People check outputs before they are used

scenes.say: When a model can’t be fixed, surround it with compensating controls. | Isolation: put it in a separate network segment, with no internet access and no new integrations. | Restricted access: named users only, strong authentication, and no anonymous use. | Modern guardrails in front: a gateway that filters inputs and validates outputs, acting as a virtual patch for weaknesses the model can’t fix itself. | Heightened monitoring: tighter thresholds, full logging and rate limits. | And human review of outputs before anyone relies on them.

scenes.title: Strict usage restrictions
scenes.say: Usage restrictions narrow what a legacy model may be used for. | Allow named, trained staff. Prohibit public or anonymous users. | Allow internal, low-sensitivity data. Prohibit personal or regulated data. | Allow approved, low-impact tasks. Prohibit automated decisions about people. | And allow use only until a fixed replacement date. Open-ended exceptions are how temporary risks become permanent.

scenes.title: A time-limited exception
scenes.say: Legacy risks are managed through a formal, time-limited exception. First, identify the gap: a weakness that can’t be fixed, or a model that can’t yet be replaced. | Assess the risk, considering exposure and consequence. | Design compensating controls that meet the intent of the control that can’t be applied. | The risk owner accepts the residual risk in writing, with an expiry date. | The controls are monitored and the exception reviewed regularly, checking that the controls still work. | And the model is replaced or retired by the agreed date, using the decommissioning process in Module 5.7.

items: Legacy models persist for cost, regulatory and dependency reasons
Isolate, restrict, guard, monitor and review
Restrict users, data, use cases and duration
Formal, time-limited exceptions owned by the risk owner
scenes.say: To recap. | Legacy models stay in service for cost, regulatory and dependency reasons, so plan for them. | Surround them with compensating controls: isolation, restricted access, modern guardrails, heightened monitoring and human review. | Restrict who may use them, with what data, for which tasks, and for how long. | And manage the remaining risk through formal, time-limited exceptions, owned by the risk owner.

blocks.md:
### What makes a control "compensating"?
A **compensating control** is an alternative measure used when a required control can’t be applied. The idea is well established: PCI DSS, for example, requires compensating controls to meet the **intent and rigour** of the original requirement, provide a similar level of defence, and go beyond other existing requirements. Apply the same test to AI: if a legacy model can’t be patched against a known jailbreak technique, a gateway that detects and blocks that technique, combined with restricted access and output review, may compensate.

### Legacy AI risks
- **Unpatched components:** old frameworks and serving stacks with known CVEs (Section 3).
- **Outdated safety behaviour:** older models are typically more susceptible to jailbreaks and injection techniques discovered since their release.
- **No vendor support:** hosted models are retired on published schedules; after retirement, nothing is fixed.
- **Missing documentation:** no model card, unknown training data and unclear limitations make risk assessment harder (Module 3.5).
- **Unsafe formats:** older models may be stored in serialisation formats that can run code when loaded; convert them to safer formats where possible.

### Designing restrictions
| Restriction | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Access** | Named user groups, strong authentication, no external or anonymous access, no new API consumers |
| **Data** | No personal, special category or regulated data; no connection to sensitive retrieval sources |
| **Use cases** | Approved tasks only; no automated decisions with legal or similar effects on people; no agentic tool use |
| **Environment** | Isolated network segment, no internet egress, read-only storage for the model |
| **Oversight** | Human review of outputs, tighter monitoring thresholds, more frequent security reviews |
| **Time** | Exception expiry and a funded replacement or retirement plan |

### Governing exceptions
Record each exception in the risk register with the gap, compensating controls, residual risk, approving risk owner, **expiry date** and review frequency. Test compensating controls as rigorously as primary ones, because they are now the only protection. Report exceptions and their ages to governance (Section 5); an exception that is renewed repeatedly is a decision to keep the risk, and should be treated as one.

blocks.title: Which compensating control fits?
pairs: The legacy model can’t be patched against a known jailbreak technique
Gateway detection and blocking of that technique
The model’s serving stack has an unfixable remote flaw
Network isolation with no external access
The model may produce unreliable outputs for some groups
Human review before outputs are used
The vendor no longer provides abuse monitoring
Organisation-run logging and tighter alert thresholds
The model was never assessed for personal data leakage
Prohibit personal data in prompts and retrieval

blocks.title: Legacy model questions
blocks.md: The best answers keep legacy models running **only with compensating controls** (isolation, restricted access, guardrails, monitoring, human review), **strict usage restrictions**, and a **time-limited exception** approved by the **risk owner**, with a replacement plan. Indefinite exceptions and "it has always worked" reasoning are traps.

q.q: A hospital relies on a legacy diagnostic support model that its vendor no longer supports. Replacement will take 18 months because of regulatory validation. What is the MOST appropriate approach?
o: Keep using it unchanged, because it was validated by the regulator originally
Restrict and isolate it, add monitoring and clinician review, under a time-limited exception
Switch it off immediately, even though clinicians depend on it for daily work
Fine-tune it on recent hospital data, so it behaves like a supported model again
q.why: Compensating controls and restrictions manage the risk while the replacement is validated, and a time-limited exception keeps accountability. Unchanged use ignores new risks, an immediate shutdown harms care, and fine-tuning would invalidate the approved version.

sections.title: Continuous security reviews and posture assurance metrics

scenes.title: Are we getting more secure?
scenes.sub: Continuous AI security reviews and posture assurance metrics
scenes.say: A security review at launch tells you how things looked on one day. AI systems, threats and usage change every week. | This video covers continuous AI security reviews, and the posture metrics that show whether security is actually improving.

scenes.title: AI security posture management
scenes.say: AI security posture management tools and processes do six things. | They discover AI assets: models, endpoints, agents, and shadow AI that nobody registered. | They map data flows, showing what each AI system can reach. | They check configurations against secure baselines. | They find attack paths: chains from an exposed endpoint, through an over-privileged identity, to sensitive data. | They prioritise risks by context and consequence. | And they track remediation, with owners, deadlines and verification.

scenes.title: A continuous review cycle
scenes.say: Continuous review runs as a cycle. Reviews are triggered by significant changes, such as a new model or new tools for an agent, by new threats, and by a schedule based on risk tier. | Each review refreshes the threat model, checks configurations and permissions, and samples the system with targeted tests. | Findings go into the vulnerability register, with owners and dates. | They are remediated: fixed, mitigated or formally accepted. | Progress is measured with posture metrics. | And results are reported to governance, which sets priorities and funding for the next cycle.

scenes.title: Posture metrics over a year
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative posture metrics for an organisation’s AI estate

series.n: AI assets with owner and current review

scenes.say: Good metrics show direction over time. In this illustrative example, the share of AI assets with a named owner and a current security review rises from forty-two per cent to ninety-one per cent over a year. | Meanwhile, the share of critical findings still open past their due date falls from thirty-eight per cent to six. Together, these show both coverage and follow-through improving.

scenes.title: Vanity metrics and meaningful metrics
rows: Share of AI assets assessed this quarter
Shadow AI use found, and its trend
scenes.say: Choose metrics that show risk, not just activity. | The number of scans run is a vanity metric. The share of AI assets actually assessed this quarter is meaningful. | Counting findings raised says little. Counting critical findings past their due date shows whether risk is being reduced. | Policies published is activity. The share of agents verified as least-privilege is outcome. | And courses completed matters less than whether shadow AI use is falling.

items: Discover assets, map flows, check configs, find attack paths
Review continuously: on change, new threats and schedule
Measure coverage, hygiene, exposure and remediation
Report meaningful metrics to governance
scenes.say: To recap. | Posture management discovers AI assets, maps data flows, checks configurations and finds attack paths. | Review continuously: on significant change, when new threats emerge, and on a risk-based schedule. | Measure coverage, hygiene, exposure and remediation. | And report meaningful metrics, not activity counts, to governance.

blocks.md:
### Continuous security reviews
- **Triggers:** new or materially changed models, new data sources or tools, new agent permissions, provider model updates, significant incidents, new threat intelligence (for example, a new injection technique), and periodic reviews by risk tier.
- **Scope:** refresh the threat model (Module 6.1), verify configurations and permissions against baselines (Module 5.1), check exposure, sample with targeted adversarial tests (Module 6.4), and confirm monitoring coverage (Module 5.2).
- **Automation:** AI security posture management (AI-SPM) and related tools continuously discover AI assets and shadow AI, check configurations, detect exposed endpoints and secrets, and map attack paths across cloud, identity and data. Use their findings as inputs to human-led reviews.
- **Continuous control monitoring:** automated tests confirm that key controls (authentication on endpoints, logging enabled, guardrails active, signed-model enforcement) are operating, not just designed.

### Posture assurance metrics
| Area | Example metrics |
|---|---|
| **Coverage** | Share of AI assets in the inventory with an owner, risk tier and current security review; shadow AI discovered |
| **Hygiene** | Share of models signed and verified; endpoints with strong authentication; agents with least-privilege verified; secrets in vaults |
| **Exposure** | Internet-facing AI endpoints; critical attack paths; open exceptions and their age |
| **Vulnerability management** | Open findings by priority; share past due date; mean time to remediate by priority |
| **Detection and response** | AI systems with monitoring in the SIEM; mean time to detect and contain AI incidents (Modules 5.2 and 5.5) |
| **Resilience** | AI systems with tested rollback and recovery; exercise findings closed (Module 5.7) |

Distinguish **key performance indicators** (how well the programme performs, such as remediation time) from **key risk indicators** (early warnings of rising risk, such as growth in internet-facing endpoints or overdue critical findings). Set targets and thresholds for each, and show trends rather than snapshots.

### Reporting and assurance
Report posture to the AI governance committee and board in business terms (Module 2.6), with clear decisions requested: funding, risk acceptance or retiring systems. Frameworks expect this loop: ISO/IEC 42001 Clause 9 (performance evaluation) and Clause 10 (improvement), the NIST AI RMF *Measure* and *Manage* functions, and the NIST CSF 2.0 *Govern* function. Internal audit and independent assessments provide further assurance that the metrics are accurate.

blocks.title: Posture terms
cards: AI-SPM
AI security posture management: continuous discovery of AI assets, configuration checks, attack path analysis and risk prioritisation.
Attack path
A chain of weaknesses an attacker could link, such as an exposed endpoint, an over-privileged identity and sensitive data.
Key risk indicator (KRI)
A metric that gives early warning of rising risk, such as overdue critical findings.
Continuous control monitoring
Automated tests that confirm key controls are operating, not just designed.
Mean time to remediate
The average time from discovering a finding to verifying its fix, tracked by priority.

blocks.title: Posture questions
blocks.md: Prefer **continuous, trigger-based reviews** over one-off launch assessments, and **outcome metrics** (coverage, past-due critical findings, least privilege verified, time to remediate) over **activity counts**. Metrics should be **trended**, have **targets**, and be reported to **governance** with decisions attached.

q.q: A CISO wants one metric to show the board whether AI vulnerability management is reducing risk. Which is MOST meaningful?
o: The total number of AI vulnerability scans run each month across the estate
The share of critical AI findings past their due date, shown as a trend
The number of AI security policies published during the last year
The total number of AI vulnerabilities discovered since the programme began
q.why: Overdue critical findings, trended over time, show whether the most important risks are actually being reduced. Scan counts, policy counts and cumulative discoveries measure activity, not risk.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a vulnerability register and an exposure register?
o: One is kept by security, the other by the legal team for regulators
One records weaknesses; the other records who can reach each AI asset
One covers models, the other covers only traditional software components
One is updated daily, the other only after each annual risk assessment
quiz.why: Weakness plus reachability gives urgency: a flaw nobody can reach matters less than one exposed to the internet.

quiz.q: Why should a register entry be retested before it is closed?
o: Retesting is required by every regulator for each AI vulnerability
To confirm the fix works, rather than trusting that a ticket was closed
To generate more findings for the next quarterly metrics report
Retesting lets the team skip assigning an owner to each entry
quiz.why: Verification proves the weakness is gone. Closed tickets alone often hide incomplete or failed fixes.

quiz.q: When is a model behaviour such as hallucination treated as a security vulnerability?
o: Always, because any incorrect output is a security failure by definition
When an attacker can reliably trigger it to cause harm or bypass a control
Never, because hallucinations are only ever a model quality issue, not security
Only when the model has been deployed for more than a year
quiz.why: Limitations become vulnerabilities when they can be exploited deliberately; otherwise they belong in quality and risk management.

quiz.q: Why can the same CVE warrant different priorities in two AI deployments?
o: CVE scores are recalculated for every organisation by the CVE Program
Exposure, data, privileges and consequence differ between deployments
Older deployments are always lower priority than newer ones
Priorities depend on which team found the vulnerability first
quiz.why: Context changes how likely exploitation is and how much harm it would cause, even when the flaw is identical.

o: The financial loss an organisation would suffer from a vulnerability
The probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days
The number of systems in the world affected by a vulnerability
The time a vendor will take to release a patch for a vulnerability
quiz.why: EPSS, from FIRST, adds a likelihood signal that base severity scores don’t provide.

quiz.q: Which factor MOST increases the urgency of patching a flaw in an AI agent platform?
o: The flaw was found by an internal team rather than an external researcher
The flaw is in CISA’s KEV catalogue and the agent is internet-facing
The platform’s vendor is headquartered in a different country from yours
The flaw has an unusually long and complicated technical description
quiz.why: Known exploitation plus exposure means attackers are likely to use the flaw against you soon.

quiz.q: Why should model evaluations be part of testing an inference framework patch?
o: Evaluations are faster to run than functional tests for most frameworks
Framework updates can subtly change model outputs and safety behaviour
Regulators require evaluations for every software change in any system
Evaluations replace the need for any functional or security testing
quiz.why: Changes to frameworks, drivers or tokenizers can shift outputs, so behaviour must be checked as well as function.

o: A patch that is downloaded automatically from the vendor’s website
A control that blocks exploitation while the real fix is prepared
A patch applied only to test environments, never to production
A simulated patch used in tabletop exercises to train staff
quiz.why: Gateway rules, network blocks or restrictions can stop exploitation of a known flaw until the fix is tested and deployed.

quiz.q: What does an AIBOM add to a traditional SBOM?
o: A list of the people who approved each software component in a build
Models, datasets and other AI-specific components and their versions
Encryption of all the component names so attackers can’t read them
The prices paid for each commercial component in the system
quiz.why: An AIBOM lets you match advisories and issues affecting models and datasets, not just software packages.

quiz.q: What makes a control a valid compensating control?
o: It is cheaper to implement than the control it replaces
It meets the intent and rigour of the requirement it replaces
It has been approved by the vendor of the legacy system
It is implemented by a different team from the original control
quiz.why: A compensating control must provide comparable protection to the control that can’t be applied, not just exist.

quiz.q: Why should exceptions for legacy models have an expiry date?
o: Expiry dates are needed so that the exception can be billed annually
Open-ended exceptions turn temporary risks into permanent ones
Models stop working when their exception expires
Regulators only allow exceptions that last exactly twelve months
quiz.why: Expiry forces a fresh decision: replace, retire or consciously renew with the risk owner’s approval.

quiz.q: Which is a meaningful posture metric rather than a vanity metric?
o: The number of AI security awareness emails sent to staff each month
The share of AI assets with an owner and a current security review
The number of vulnerability scanning tools the organisation licenses
The total number of pages in the organisation’s AI security policy
quiz.why: Coverage of assets by ownership and review reflects actual control over risk, unlike activity counts.

quiz.q: What does AI security posture management typically do?
o: Train new models with improved safety behaviour for the organisation
Discover AI assets, check configurations and find attack paths
Replace the need for human security reviews of AI systems
Negotiate security terms in contracts with AI providers
quiz.why: AI-SPM provides continuous visibility of assets, misconfigurations and attack paths, feeding human-led reviews and remediation.

exam.q: A red team finds that a customer assistant can be made to reveal internal pricing rules through role-play prompts. The finding is noted in a slide deck, but no one owns it, and three months later it is still exploitable. What is the BEST process improvement?
o: Ask the red team to present its findings more forcefully at the next review
Record findings in a register with an owner, due date and retest before closure
Remove the role-play capability from every model used anywhere in the organisation
Reduce the frequency of red team exercises, so fewer findings are left open
exam.why: A register with ownership, deadlines and verification turns findings into fixes. Presentation style, blanket capability bans and fewer exercises don’t create accountability.

exam.q: A vulnerability with a CVSS base score of 6.5 affects the vector database behind an internal HR assistant that retrieves salary and disciplinary records. EPSS is high, and exploit code is public. How should it be prioritised?
o: Low, because its base score is below the organisation’s critical threshold
High, because exploitation is likely and the records are highly sensitive
Low, because the assistant is internal and employees are trusted users
Defer, until the vendor rates the vulnerability as critical in an update
exam.why: Likely exploitation combined with highly sensitive data raises the contextual priority well above the base score. Internal systems still face insider and compromised-account threats.

exam.q: Which approach to vulnerability prioritisation BEST suits an organisation with hundreds of AI deployments and limited staff?
o: Fix vulnerabilities strictly in order of CVSS base score, highest first
Combine exploitation data, exposure, data sensitivity and consequence
Fix the vulnerabilities in the oldest systems first, whatever their risk
Let each development team decide which findings to fix, if any
exam.why: Risk-based prioritisation focuses scarce effort where exploitation is likely and harm would be greatest. Base-score ordering, age and team preference ignore context.

exam.q: A new release of a popular agent orchestration library fixes a flaw that allows code execution through crafted tool outputs. The organisation uses the library in 30 services, but nobody is sure which versions. What should be done FIRST?
o: Wait for each service team to notice the advisory and upgrade when convenient
Use SBOM data to identify affected services and versions, then prioritise patching
Upgrade all 30 services immediately in production without any testing
Ban the library from future projects and leave existing services as they are
exam.why: Identifying exactly where vulnerable versions run is the first step to prioritised, tested patching. Waiting, untested mass upgrades and future-only bans all leave risk unmanaged.

exam.q: After a GPU driver and framework update, a fraud model’s outputs shift slightly, and its false negative rate rises by 3 points. The update passed all functional tests. What does this show?
o: Functional tests are unnecessary and can be dropped for future updates
Patch testing must include model evaluations, not just functional tests
GPU driver updates should never be applied to AI systems running in production
The fraud model should be retrained after every infrastructure change
exam.why: Infrastructure changes can alter model behaviour, so evaluations must be part of patch testing. Dropping functional tests, avoiding driver patches or routine retraining are wrong lessons.

exam.q: A manufacturer’s quality inspection model runs on an unsupported serving stack with a known remote code execution flaw. Replacement is scheduled in nine months. Which approach BEST manages the risk meanwhile?
o: Accept the risk informally, because the replacement is already scheduled
Isolate and restrict it, with monitoring, under a time-limited exception
Disable the model now and inspect all products manually for nine months
Ask the original vendor to support the stack again for one more year
exam.why: Isolation, restricted access and monitoring reduce exploitability, and a formal exception keeps the risk owned until replacement. Informal acceptance, disruptive shutdowns and hoping for vendor support don’t manage the risk.

exam.q: A legacy chatbot can’t be updated to resist newer jailbreak techniques. The business wants to extend it to anonymous public users. What should the security team advise?
o: Approve the extension, because the chatbot has worked well for its internal users
Keep it to named internal users, with gateway guardrails, until it is replaced
Approve the extension, but add a disclaimer that answers may be inaccurate
Retrain the chatbot on public data so that it is ready for external users
exam.why: A model that can’t resist known techniques should not gain a larger, anonymous attack surface. Restrictions and guardrails contain it until replacement; disclaimers and retraining on public data don’t fix the weakness.

exam.q: An organisation reviewed each AI system’s security only at launch. Two years later, many agents have gained new tools and data sources. What should it introduce?
o: A second launch review for each system, held once at the two-year anniversary
Trigger-based and risk-tiered reviews, supported by continuous posture checks
A rule that AI systems can never gain new tools after their launch review
An annual survey asking system owners whether anything important has changed
exam.why: Reviews triggered by significant change and scheduled by risk tier, with continuous automated checks, keep assessments current. One-off reviews, change freezes and surveys don’t.

exam.q: The board receives a monthly AI security report listing scans run, policies published and training completed. Which change would make it MOST useful for decision-making?
o: Add more activity counts, such as meetings held and emails sent to staff
Replace activity counts with trended outcome metrics and decisions required
Remove all metrics, and present a narrative summary from the CISO instead
Send the report weekly instead of monthly, so the board sees more data
exam.why: Boards need outcome metrics trended against targets, with clear decisions to make. More activity data, no data or more frequent reports don’t support decisions.
